timeline.event: Friedrich Ernst's land grant at Industry, Austin County: first permanent German settlement in Texas (inside MSA)
Robert Justus Kleberg imports a piano and music books to Harrisburg (now Houston): earliest reference to music among Texas German immigrants
Ball for Stephen F. Austin at Jane Long's former boarding house in Brazoria; 1,000 colonists attend.
Battle of San Jacinto (Harris Co.): by tradition Texans march to 'Will You Come to the Bower?'; Czech fifer Frederick Lemsky plays in the Texas band
San Jacinto Victory Ball in Houston; Sam Houston leads the grand march.
Mary Austin Holley hears Germans singing on a Galveston-Houston boat; 1839 German soirees at Kessler's Arcade; 1840 Emil Heerbrugger violin/horn/guitar recitals in Houston
Mid-1840s: informal German singing groups in Galveston and Houston, then the Houston Manner-Gesangverein
German Quartette Society formed in Houston (roots of the Saengerbund, formally founded 1883)
First organized Czech emigrant group sets out (Aug 19); Galveston becomes port of entry and Cat Spring (Austin Co.) the dispersal point
Cat Spring Agricultural Society founded (Austin Co.); later known for June Fest and its 12-sided hall
General Order No. 3 read in Galveston, June 19: the origin of Juneteenth
Freedmen led by Rev. Jack Yates buy 10 acres for $800 to celebrate emancipation: Emancipation Park
Millheim Harmonie Verein hall built (verein founded 1872).
Houston Sangerbund founded
Bellville Turnverein Pavilion, first round dance hall in Texas.
Cat Spring Agricultural Society Hall built.
Imperial State Prison Farm opens at Sugar Land (convict leasing on the Imperial Sugar land from 1878); renamed Central State Prison Farm 1930
SPJST Lodge 88 organized in Houston by the Czechoslovak club Pokrok
Lead Belly transferred to Imperial Farm, Sugar Land (May 1920); pardoned 1925 after a song for Gov. Pat Neff
Louisiana Creoles organize Frenchtown in Houston's Fifth Ward, later the cradle of urban zydeco
Houston jailbreak later worked into Lead Belly's 'Midnight Special'; Lomaxes tie the song's train to Houston and the Sugar Land prison
Frenchtown's Our Mother of Mercy church opens (June 9), funded partly by la-la dances
Mendoza family (Lydia, later NEA Heritage Fellow) returns to Houston and plays Magnolia Park
Jimmie Rodgers records Shelly Lee Alley's 'Travelin' Blues' with Shelly and Alvin Alley on twin fiddles
December: Lomaxes record Lightnin' Washington's group at Darrington State Prison, Sandy Point (Brazoria) and Iron Head Baker ('The Grey Goose') at Central State Farm, Sugar Land
October: Lomaxes return to Central State Farm; Iron Head, Will Crosby, Mose 'Clear Rock' Platt and R. D. Allen record 'The Gray Goose'
c. 1934-35: Houston-born fiddler Leon 'Pappy' Selph forms the Blue Ridge Playboys (Floyd Tillman, Moon Mullican, Ted Daffan) with a KPRC radio show
Fiddler Cliff Bruner forms the Texas Wanderers in Houston (KXYZ); Shelly Lee Alley forms the Alley Cats (Houston/Beaumont)
April: John and Ruby Lomax record at Clemens State Farm (Smith Casey, 'Clemens Rag') and Ramsey State Farm Camp 4, Otey (Stavin' Chain singers), Brazoria Co.
October: Bill Quinn opens Quinn Recording, later Gold Star (1950) and SugarHill (1970s)
John Henry Faulk records work songs and blues by Black prisoners at Sugarland for the Archive of American Folk Song
Don Robey opens the Bronze Peacock Dinner Club
Cajun fiddler Harry Choates records 'Jole Blon' for Gold Star in Houston, the only Cajun song to reach Billboard's Top 5; Lightnin' Hopkins discovered on Dowling Street
Dr. Carl Journell begins square dance classes; Square Dance Council of the Houston Area formed; HIFD founded.
c. 1947: Hopkins's 'Zolo Go' (Gold Star) first record to use a variant of 'zydeco' for a music style; Clarence Garlow's 'Bon Ton Roula' (1949) second, both Houston
First Square Dance Spring Festival at Sam Houston Coliseum: 9,950 attendees, 60+ clubs, ~5,000 members.
Don Robey founds Peacock Records; its gospel division (Dixie Hummingbirds, Sensational Nightingales, Mighty Clouds of Joy) keeps the label afloat
Willie Green's Christmas Eve set at Irene's Cafe brings Creole accordion music into public venues

June: Houston Folklore Society founded by John A. Lomax Jr., Ed Badeaux, Howie Porper, Chester Bower, Harold Belikoff; c. 1951 Johnson's Lounge (later Continental Zydeco Ballroom) hires Lonnie Mitchell
First rodeo trail ride (Brenham to Houston), the start of the Salt Grass Trail Ride
Spring Festival attendance ~25,000.
Big Mama Thornton's 'Hound Dog' on Peacock; Robey takes over Duke Records
Merrbach studio launches Blue Star Records in the Heights.
1956-58: Mance Lipscomb lives in Houston, playing bars against Lightnin' Hopkins
Prairie View Trail Riders founded, the rodeo's first African American trail ride
Mack McCormick records Hopkins's 'Autobiography in Blues'; McCormick's transcription fixes the spelling 'zydeco' (album dated 1959 in one Handbook entry, 1960 in another)
McCormick records 200+ Fourth Ward 'Santa Fe' barrelhouse pianists while a census taker; with Chris Strachwitz finds Mance Lipscomb in Navasota (outside MSA)
Jester Lounge opens at 2509 Midlane (Mac Webster); Tex-i-an Boys (HFS spin-off) release 'Songs of Texas' on Folkways
HFS concert series at the Jewish Community Center begins with Ed Badeaux and Mance Lipscomb (Feb 15)
Alfred Cormier opens Alfred's Place (later Silver Slipper) in Frenchtown, zydeco and blues six nights a week
Houston Highlanders Pipes & Drums formed
Chris Strachwitz hears Clifton Chenier in Houston and records him the next day; McCormick records Robert Shaw
Chenier records 'Zydeco Sont Pas Sale' at Gold Star for Arhoolie; Bruce Jackson begins Texas prison work-song recordings (1964-66), including Ramsey Unit (Brazoria)
Hey Lollies square dance club founded.
Old Quarter opens downtown near Congress and Austin streets in a former speakeasy (Rex "Wrecks" Bell and Cecil Slayton)
May: Sand Mountain Coffee House opens at 1213 Richmond (founded by teens John Carrick and Steve Gladson with $170); McCormick's Almanac label; McCormick drives ex-convicts to Newport
Jester Lounge closes; HFS newsletter begins (June); Seegers and Bruce Jackson film work songs at Ellis Unit, Huntsville (outside MSA)
Square dance festival switches from live bands to records; Camping Squares formed.
First Original Greek Festival (inferred from 59th in 2025)
HFS newsletter renamed Cotton Patch Rag (still published); McCormick cultural historian for Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife featuring Texas
Fiestas Patrias parade founded by Judge Armando V. Rodriguez
Anderson Fair founded as a restaurant at 2007 Grant St., Montrose (the club says music since 1970; music focus by 1973)

Arlo Guthrie plays 'Alice's Restaurant' live as KPFT returns to the air (Jan 21)
'Main Street 1' arts happening, seed of the Houston International Festival; liquor by the drink legalized, songwriters move toward bars
Gulf Coast Scandinavian Folk Dancers (later Scandinavian Folkdancers of Houston) organized.
First Kerrville Folk Festival (outside MSA) with Townes Van Zandt and Mance Lipscomb; John Lomax Jr. sang at the first two
Townes Van Zandt records Live at the Old Quarter (July; released 1977)
Robey sells Duke-Peacock to ABC-Dunhill; Curley Cormier takes over the Silver Slipper
Texas Renaissance Festival founded at Todd Mission (outside MSA); John Lomax Jr. dies Dec 12 in Houston
Sand Mountain Coffee House closes
MECA founded; Festival Chicano organized (1977 per UNT oral history, 1979 per houstonse)

Late 1970s (HATDS) or 1980 (Dorcas Hand's own CDSS account): contra dancing brought to Houston by Dorcas Hand and Barry Cooper, sometimes danced in driveways

Clifton Chenier named an NEA National Heritage Fellow
North Harris County Dulcimer Society founded with 10 people in a private home
Spring Festival (moved to fall) renamed Houston Hoedown.

35th National Square Dance Convention at the Astrodome: 20,164 dancers.

Fort Bend Songwriters Association founded in Richmond (later the Houston Songwriters Association)
Accordion Kings & Queens begins at Miller Outdoor Theatre (per Texas Folklife)
Houston Accordion Association founded
McGonigel's Mucky Duck grand opening June 1 (Rusty Andrews); HATDS incorporated Sept 14
CFMA Houston Heritage Chapter incorporated in Texas (later forfeited)
Celtic band Clandestine (pipes, fiddle, guitar, bodhran) forms in Houston
Millbend Coffeehouse's first show (December, the Banded Geckos)

Rex Bell opens the Old Quarter Acoustic Cafe in Galveston
Kaminari Taiko founded

costs.notes: HATDS contra: $15 non-member, $10 member, $5 ages 18-30, free under 18; Thursday experiment $5 flat. Bayou Bedlam 2026 $150 ($60 ages 18-30, $35 single session). HIFD free 25 and under. RSCDS $8 members; Ball $45. SPJST Lodge 88 dances $15-20; Needville $10. Jax Grill zydeco nights are restaurant events (no published cover). HFMS Second Saturday $20 suggested; Millbend Coffeehouse $25; Anderson Fair $15 (Thursday showcase) to $20-30 (shows), cash bar; Old Quarter tickets plus $10 at the door; Coffee House Houston free (donations); Mucky Duck open mic free; Sacred Harp singings free; HFMS dues $20/$35; Fulshear and Champions house concerts $30 donation (100% to the artist)

surprises: Zydeco dwarfs every other participatory form: one promoter-fed calendar (ZydecoEvents.com) lists at least 21-30 separate zydeco dance dates a month in the MSA, and Jax Grill on Shepherd Dr has had live zydeco every Friday and Saturday for 25+ years, roughly 104 dance nights a year against about 30 for Houston's whole contra series.

'Zydeco' is a Houston word: the first two records to use a variant of it for a music (Lightnin' Hopkins' 'Zolo Go', c. 1947, and Clarence Garlow's 'Bon Ton Roula', 1949) were made in Houston, and Houston folklorist Mack McCormick fixed the spelling in 1959/60 (Handbook of Texas).

A Black Catholic church-dance circuit still runs: at least 7 of the 11 parishes Texas Monthly listed around 1988 hosted zydeco dances, matinees or bazaars in 2025-26, many organized by the Knights of Peter Claver, including a 'Zydeco Breakfast Dance'.
One Knights of Columbus hall (Roemer Hall, 607 E Whitney St, with a sprung floor) hosts the Bayou Bedlam contra weekend, a Black trail riders' zydeco kickoff dance and Czech polka dinner-dances.

One Midtown church, First Lutheran at 1311 Holman St, hosts contra, English country dance, international folk dance, Scottish country dance and Sacred Harp: about 15 events a month in five traditions.

Square dancing went from 9,950 people at the 1949 Coliseum festival and 20,164 dancers at the 1987 National Convention in the Astrodome to 230 at the 2026 Houston Hoedown, yet its 12 clubs still list about 48 club nights a month, the largest non-zydeco category.
Sunday football has evicted Houston's Irish session again and again: from three pubs in a row before about 2005, then The Harp, then Pimlico in 2019 ('perhaps we'll be back after football season').

The Bay Area Bluegrass Association cancelled its remaining 2026 shows on Oct 5, 2026 after 40 years ('no longer sustainable'), while the bluegrass jams around it run at about 17 a month, three of them weekly.
A Houston Irish session publishes its own data: ceol.app holds 38 dated Sunday sessions at Hugh O'Connor's (Nov 2025-Oct 2026) with 96 distinct tunes; the most-logged tune is 'The Diplodocus'.

Old-time arrived late: in 2013 a local said there were 'no strictly Old Time jams' in Houston; the 2026 jam's theme list (Cherry River Rag, L&N Rag, Denver Belle, Texas Fair) leans Texan and ragtime, not Round Peak.

No Texas-style fiddle contest is held inside the 9-county MSA, in the state that made contest fiddling; the 'World Champion Fiddlers Festival' is on Houston Avenue in Crockett, Houston County, 120 miles north.
'Jole Blon', the only Cajun record ever to reach Billboard's Top 5 in any category, was cut in Houston at Gold Star in 1946 by fiddler Harry Choates, who sold it for $100 and a bottle of whiskey.

The Ku Klux Klan bombed KPFT's transmitter twice in 1970, the second time while it was playing 'Alice's Restaurant'; Arlo Guthrie came in to play the song live when the station returned in January 1971.

Lomax field-recording sites lie inside the MSA: the Sugar Land prison farm where Lead Belly served (1920-25) and where the Lomaxes recorded Iron Head Baker in 1933-34 is now a master-planned suburb, and four Brazoria County prison farms were recorded in 1933-39.

Austin County, at the MSA's western edge, holds 7 of Texas's 18 known 'round' dance halls; the prototype, the 12-sided Bellville Turnverein Pavilion (1897), cost $360 and its 2023 restoration hid the air conditioning under the dance floor.
curiosities: Is Houston the largest zydeco dance city outside Louisiana? Compare listed zydeco dates per month with Lafayette/Opelousas and with Creole diaspora scenes in Los Angeles, the Bay Area and Chicago.

Do other metros have a parish-hall dance circuit for a vernacular music (Black Catholic zydeco in Houston; polka Masses in Milwaukee or Cleveland; Czech parish picnics in Texas), and how do their sizes and ages compare?
Is the Irish session's 'evicted by Sunday football' pattern unique to Texas, or do Sunday sessions in other NFL cities show the same seasonal fragility?
How do modern Western square dance decline curves compare across metros (Houston: 100+ clubs in the late 1940s, 12 in 2026), and what is the ratio of MWSD nights to contra nights in each city?

Why does a 7.9-million metro sustain only one contra series (about 3 dances a month) when smaller metros dance weekly? Heat, sprawl, a late start (1980 vs Austin or Dallas), or competition from zydeco and two-step?
Bluegrass jam-meetings and Irish session-meetings run about 1:1 in Houston (about 17 vs 16 a month). How does that ratio vary across the 20 metros, and does it track Southern identity?

Why is there no Cajun jam in Houston, the main destination of Louisiana out-migration, when Cajun jams thrive 2-3 hours east? Did migrants fold into zydeco and country dance instead, and is the same true in Dallas and Los Angeles?
Why do Texas-style fiddle contests avoid the big metros (none in the Houston MSA)? Does the same urban-rural split hold for fiddlers' conventions in Virginia, North Carolina and the Midwest?
Why is son jarocho visible in Los Angeles, the Bay Area, Chicago and San Antonio but untraceable in Houston, which has one of the largest Mexican American populations?
Is a single 'folk-dance church' hosting four or more traditions (First Lutheran in Houston) common in other metros, and what makes a hall become one (rent, floor, air conditioning, denomination)?
Why do port cities like Seattle, San Francisco and Boston have monthly shanty sings while Houston and Galveston (home of the 1877 barque Elissa) have none?

How many large metros have three or more monthly Sacred Harp singings, and what share started after 2004 (Houston's first recorded singing)? Is the urban Sun Belt revival separate from the rural Texas conventions?
Which other top-20 metros contain Library of Congress / Lomax field-recording sites inside their MSA, as Houston does with the Sugar Land and Brazoria prison farms?
Are other cities' bluegrass associations losing their show series to aging volunteers while their jams stay healthy, as BABA did in October 2026?

How many US folk societies founded before 1955 still publish a newsletter (HFMS, 1951, Cotton Patch Rag vol. 61), and how many volunteer-run listening rooms have survived 50+ years like Anderson Fair?
Could public tune logs (ceol.app) give a cross-city 'most played tunes' dataset to compare Houston's sessions with Boston's or Seattle's?
data_quality_notes:
MERGE AND DEDUPE (Oct 30, 2026): five research threads (sessions, dance, song, heritage, history) were merged. Cross-thread duplicates were collapsed into single records, keeping the freshest last_evidence, the higher confidence and the union of notes: Jax Grill, Club Menai, Prospect Park, the Catholic parish zydeco circuit, the trail-ride dance aggregate, ASLD zydeco lessons, Step N Class, SPJST Lodge 88, Needville SPJST, Sealy Lions, Wallis "Let's Dance", the Houston Accordion Association; also duplicate venues (First Lutheran, Jax, Needville hall, Peters Hall), organizations (Gulf Coast Cruinniú, CFMA Houston chapter), festivals (Cruinniú x3, Accordion Kings & Queens, Original Greek Festival, Bayou Bedlam, Highland Games), archives (Rice x3, McCormick, HFMS audio), heritage traditions (zydeco x3, Czech/German dance halls, German singing x3, Black gospel quartet x3, Cajun, Juneteenth, Greek, Scottish, Scandinavian), people (Dorcas Hand, Rusty Andrews), defunct (Continental Zydeco Ballroom x3, Silver Slipper, Red Lion, Balladeer/La Maison) and 24 duplicate timeline entries.

CENSUS RULES APPLIED: events without dated 2024-26 evidence are kept but counted at 0 (Houston Accordion Association, Fort Bend Accordion Club; flagged unverified) or moved to instruction (Step N Class, undated page). Annual concerts and festivals were removed from the events list and kept in festivals (Kerrville New Folk showcase at the Mucky Duck, Townes Van Zandt Wake, Bellville Sängerfest); participatory annual events stay at 0.083/month (Houston All-Day Sacred Harp Singing, Primm Birthday Singing, Houston Céilí at 0.17). A performance team (Lollie Cloggers) moved to organizations. BABA's monthly show is counted at 0 after its Oct 5, 2026 cancellation. Listening-series concerts (HFMS Second Saturday, Millbend, Coffee House Houston, two house-concert series, Gospel Songfest) are counted as "other"/"heritage" events because they are recurring and public, but they are listening, not participatory. Five events outside the 9 counties are flagged outside_msa and excluded from totals (Fayetteville picking and polka, Brenham polka, Coldspring and Plantersville jams).

SANITY CHECKS: Square dance (48.7/month) was checked against the HSRDC club table fetched Oct 30, 2026: all 11 weekly clubs list a weekly night (The Woodlands Stars alternate Mainstream/Plus and DBD; Tim's Gems is a Plus workshop on 1st Tuesdays and Advanced otherwise; Camping Squares is monthly). The figure is the listed-schedule ceiling; summer and holiday breaks probably reduce real club nights by 10-20%, and many are class or workshop nights. Heritage community events fell from 66/month in the naive merge (double-counted zydeco and dance-hall records) to about 35/month; zydeco alone (including ASLD lessons) is about 35/month, consistent with the ZydecoEvents floor of 21-30 listed dates plus the weekly rooms that the calendar under-lists. Club Menai (2.5), Prospect Park (3) and the trail-ride aggregate (1.5) were set between the two threads' estimates; Big Easy Sunday zydeco (4.33) rests on the venue's own claim (site description modified Oct 28, 2026) while ZydecoEvents shows only six Big Easy listings.

CONTRADICTIONS BETWEEN SOURCES: Crockett fiddlers festival month (Handbook: June; 2026 edition Nov 13-14, confirmed by a web check, so it moved); Mucky Duck opening (1987 online vs 1990 per the owner, 1990 used); Anderson Fair (1969 restaurant vs 1970 music); contra arrival (HATDS late 1970s vs Dorcas Hand's 1980); Accordion Kings & Queens ("since 1989" vs 37th in 2026); Festival Chicano (1977 vs 1979); Original Greek Festival (1966 vs 1967, 1967 used); Silver Slipper (1952 vs 1962); McCormick's zydeco spelling (1959 vs 1960); Chenier's move to Houston (1946/47 vs 1960s); Prairie View Trail Riders founder and year (1957/58; HPM's 1975 likely a typo); Club Menai street (Homestead Ct vs Rd); Houston Accordion Association day (3rd vs 2nd Tuesday); HATDS Saturdays (contradancelinks 1st/3rd, stale; HATDS 2nd/4th used); which trail-riders association holds the KC Hall #2917 kickoff (Southwest vs Southwestern); Wikipedia's claim that Houston hosted the 1951 National Folk Festival (contradicted by the NCTA list, which puts it in St. Louis 1947-55); ZydecoEvents counts (dance thread at least 21/month over 22 months with pagination capped; heritage thread about 30/month over 10 months); Texas Fasola numbering the 2026 all-day singing "18th" though the 16th was in 2019.

DISTINCT TRADITIONS ACTIVE = 28: 20 traditions with a verified 2024-26 recurring participatory practice in the MSA (Irish sessions; Irish céilí/step; bluegrass; old-time incl. dulcimer; blues jam; contra; English country/historical; MWSD squares/rounds/clogging; Scottish country dance; international folk dance; Israeli; Sacred Harp; folk song circles/singer-songwriter; gospel quartet; German-Texan choral; zydeco; Czech/German-Texan polka halls; mariachi; ballet folklórico; conjunto/Tejano) plus 8 with dated 2024-26 ensemble or festival activity backed by a living practice (Scottish piping; powwow; Indian classical and garba; Slavic folk-dance ensembles; Greek dance; Caribbean mas and steelpan; Lebanese dabke; West African). Excluded for lack of dated evidence or of a participatory practice: Cajun (radio and festival bands only, no community dance or jam), danza azteca, Chinese traditional orchestra, taiko, Brazilian capoeira/samba, Vietnamese, Korean, Filipino, Garifuna, Hawaiian, klezmer (gig bands only), Scandinavian, son jarocho (not found), shanty singing (none participatory). The naive merge's 60 counted free-text event traditions and was not meaningful.

COVERAGE GAPS: private Facebook groups ("Irish Sessions Houston", "Greater Houston Old Time Music", "Where The Zydeco @ Texas?") limit verification of cancellations; the Black gospel quartet anniversary circuit is real but uncounted; Houston Chronicle, KHOU and UH Libraries pages often returned 403 or paywalls (search snippets used); tunearch.org, slippery-hill.com and si.edu blocked direct fetches (tune notes medium confidence); web search was rate-limited during several threads. Membership counts are unpublished except HIFD (~75, undated). Not found or unverified: any Scottish/Cape Breton, Cajun, Western swing, gypsy jazz, klezmer, Balkan or Scandinavian open session; any Texas-style fiddle jam or contest in the MSA; a public shanty sing, ballad group, Christian Harmony singing or cowboy-poetry gathering; son jarocho; Comhaltas "Róisín Buí den Texas"; Houston Scottish Fiddle Club; Shanty-Chor Houston after 2014; CFMA Houston chapter after 2005; Scandinavian Folkdancers after 1998; Clear Lake ECD and SCA venues; Old Quarter song-circle and Anderson Fair showcase frequencies; Lomax recordings at Retrieve State Farm. Coordinates exist only for some events (TheSession and Nominatim); several are street- or town-level approximations.
nutshell: Houston's folk scene is big, sprawling and split into worlds that rarely meet. By volume its signature is Creole zydeco: Jax Grill has had live zydeco every Friday and Saturday for 25-plus years, Black Catholic parishes still hold church-hall dances and bazaars, and Black trail-riding clubs end their campouts with zydeco bands. One promoter calendar alone lists 21 to 30 zydeco dance dates a month. Alongside it run 12 modern Western square dance clubs (about 48 club nights a month, down from 100-plus clubs in 1949), a suburban bluegrass jam network (about 17 a month), a compact Irish session cluster near Rice Village (about 16), and a small, 40-year-old revival scene of contra, English, Scottish and international dance centered on one Midtown church. The song side is the Texas singer-songwriter tradition of the Jester, Sand Mountain, the Old Quarter and Anderson Fair, tended since 1951 by a volunteer folk society. West of town, Czech and German halls still hold monthly polka dances.
